sections.body: Some stress before exams can help focus. Too much makes it hard to think, sleep or eat.
What helps: a realistic revision plan with breaks, active recall (testing yourself), sleep (cramming all night hurts memory), exercise, and talking about worries.
Results matter, but they don't define your worth. There are many paths to a good life and career.
If stress feels overwhelming or you feel hopeless, talk to someone now: a parent, teacher, counsellor, doctor or a youth helpline. In an emergency, call your local emergency number.

quiz.q: Which revision approach is best for memory?
options: Short sessions with breaks and self-testing
hints: Your brain needs rest to store memories.
Athletes train in sessions with rest days, not one 20-hour workout.
quiz.explain: Spaced sessions with breaks and self-testing work best, and sleep helps you remember.

quiz.q: A friend says they feel hopeless about exams and can't cope. What should you do?
options: Listen, take it seriously, and help them talk to a trusted adult
Tell them to stop being dramatic
hints: If a friend twisted their ankle badly, you'd help them get to someone who can treat it.
quiz.explain: Listen, take it seriously, and help them reach a trusted adult or professional.

quiz.q: Which statement about stress before exams matches the lesson?
options: Some stress can help you focus, but too much makes it hard to think, sleep or eat
Any stress before an exam means something is wrong with you
The more stressed you feel, the better you'll perform
hints: Is stress described as always good, always bad, or something in between?
The lesson contrasts a little stress with too much stress.
Worked example: a guitar string needs some tension to play a note, but too little and it's floppy, and too much and it can snap. The amount changes the effect.
quiz.explain: A moderate amount of stress can sharpen focus, but too much makes it hard to think, sleep or eat. If stress feels overwhelming, use the coping strategies in the lesson and talk to someone you trust.
